title: Ethiopia and Eritrea edge toward war
deck: Two former enemies that made peace in 2018 cut ties, trade accusations at the UN Security Council and fight over Tigray, with a Red Sea port and millions of hungry civilians in the middle.

card.headline: Ethiopia says Eritrean troops are inside Tigray; Eritrea calls that a 'declaration of war'

keyNumber.label: how far Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on 9 October that Eritrean troops had advanced into Tigray (a claim, not independently verified here)

forYou.line: Ethiopian coffee and other cargo face route and insurance risk. Check where your Red Sea-linked freight actually goes.
Another Red Sea flashpoint on top of the Iran-war freight shock. Treat it as a tail risk to shipping costs, not yet a market event.
Roughly 4 million people in Tigray need urgent help, and the fighting is cutting across access routes.
Watch whether a border-and-port dispute becomes a full state-to-state war. That is the line that changes the outlook.

whatHappened: Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on 9 October 2026 that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 km into Tigray. It invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which covers self-defence.
On 10 October Eritrea replied that this amounted to a 'declaration of war'. It said Addis Ababa wants to seize the Red Sea port of Assab.

On the ground, federal forces retook Mekelle on 3-4 October and Adigrat on 10 October from a TPLF-led alliance of seven rebel groups formed in September. The two states had severed diplomatic ties on 1 October. Roughly 4 million people in Tigray need urgent aid.
whyItMatters: The Tigray war of 2020-22 ended with the Pretoria agreement in November 2022. This is the most serious sign yet that the settlement is failing, and that it could pull in a second state.
Assab is a Red Sea port, and Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea's independence. A fight over access to the sea touches shipping lanes that are already under strain from the Iran war.
The humanitarian cost is immediate. About 4 million people need urgent aid, and the same donors and agencies are stretched by famine alerts in Sudan.

winners.why: Fighting between two armed states raises demand for weapons and force protection. We have no sourced figures.

winners.who: Gulf states with Red Sea ambitions (UAE, Saudi)
winners.why: A weakened or distracted Horn of Africa gives patrons more leverage over port and security deals. This is our judgement, not a sourced finding.
War framing silences domestic critics and justifies tighter control. This is a general pattern, not a claim from our sources.

losers.why: About 4 million need urgent aid, and frontline fighting makes delivery harder.
Conflict raises transport, insurance and payment risk for the country's best-known export.
A Tigray-Eritrea war would push refugees and arms into eastern Sudan and divert aid logistics from Darfur and Kordofan, where famine risk is rising.
A second flashpoint near the Red Sea approach adds to freight costs that have been elevated since February.

whatsNext: Watch for further Security Council meetings or a statement. Neither Ethiopia's Article 51 claim nor Eritrea's reply has produced one yet in our sources.
Watch for a battle for the Tigray-Eritrea border zone and any move toward Assab or the Eritrean coast.
Watch for mediation by the African Union or regional states, and whether either government restores contact.
Watch whether the TPLF-led alliance holds together after losing Mekelle and Adigrat.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely path over the next six months?
options: Frozen standoff with continued insurgency in Tigray
Open war between the Ethiopian and Eritrean armies
Quick federal consolidation and an Eritrean pullback
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 40%, is a frozen standoff. Fighting continues in Tigray, rhetoric stays hot and the border is tense, but neither capital commits to a full interstate war. Open war is the second most likely path at about 25%. These are author judgements, not sourced forecasts.

timeline.title: Pretoria agreement ends the first Tigray war
timeline.detail: Federal government and Tigrayan authorities sign a cessation of hostilities. Eritrean troops, who had fought in Tigray, were not party to it.

timeline.title: Seven-group rebel alliance formed (September)
timeline.detail: A TPLF-led alliance of seven groups forms against the federal government. The exact date is not in our sources; the first of the month is a placeholder.

timeline.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea sever diplomatic ties
timeline.detail: The two states break relations, ending the formal links that followed the 2018 peace deal.

timeline.title: Federal forces retake Mekelle (3-4 October)
timeline.detail: Tigray's regional capital changes hands, according to the event summary.

timeline.title: Ethiopia tells the UN Eritrean troops advanced up to 60 km into Tigray
timeline.detail: Addis Ababa invokes Article 51 of the UN Charter in a letter or address to the Security Council.

timeline.title: Eritrea calls it a 'declaration of war'; Adigrat retaken
timeline.detail: Eritrea accuses Ethiopia of seeking to seize the port of Assab. Federal forces retake Adigrat the same day.

timeline.title: The New Humanitarian reports fears of a wider regional war
timeline.detail: Analysis of Eritrean incursions into Tigray and what they mean for the region.

causes.name: Unfinished Pretoria settlement
causes.detail: The 2022 agreement ended open war in Tigray but did not settle who holds power there or what role Eritrea would play.

causes.name: Landlocked Ethiopia and the Red Sea
causes.detail: Ethiopia has no coastline and has pressed for sea access. Eritrea reads that as a threat to Assab.

causes.name: Eritrea's militarised state
causes.detail: Eritrea's leadership sees Ethiopia's moves on the coast and in Tigray as security threats.

causes.name: Rebel alliance forms
causes.detail: A seven-group TPLF-led alliance forms in September and the federal government moves against it.

causes.name: Diplomatic rupture
causes.detail: Ties are severed on 1 October, removing a channel for managing incidents.

causes.name: Fall of Mekelle and Adigrat
causes.detail: Federal advances put forces close to the Eritrean border.

causes.name: Reported Eritrean incursions
causes.detail: Ethiopia says Eritrean troops advanced up to 60 km into Tigray and takes the case to the UN.

causes.name: Distracted great powers
causes.detail: US attention is on the Iran war, which leaves Gulf patrons and regional actors more room to act.

stakeholders.name: Abiy Ahmed's government
stakeholders.wants: Defeat the TPLF-led alliance, secure the north and keep Red Sea access on the agenda
stakeholders.leverage: Larger army, UN platform, Article 51 argument
stakeholders.likelyMove: Press the diplomatic case at the UN while consolidating control of Tigray's towns

stakeholders.name: Isaias Afwerki's government
stakeholders.wants: Prevent any Ethiopian move on Assab; keep Tigray weak and divided
stakeholders.leverage: Experienced, mobilised forces; control of the coast
stakeholders.likelyMove: Frame Ethiopia as the aggressor and keep forces forward in border areas

stakeholders.name: TPLF-led seven-group alliance
stakeholders.wants: Survive the loss of Mekelle and Adigrat and hold the alliance together
stakeholders.likelyMove: Shift to insurgency; seek outside backing

stakeholders.name: Tigrayan civilians and aid agencies
stakeholders.likelyMove: Appeal for corridors; scale back where convoys are unsafe

stakeholders.name: UN Security Council members
stakeholders.wants: Avoid a wider war without taking sides
stakeholders.likelyMove: Call for restraint and talks; slow to act

stakeholders.name: Gulf patrons (UAE, Saudi)
stakeholders.wants: Influence over Red Sea ports and security arrangements
stakeholders.likelyMove: Quiet diplomacy and support to preferred partners

sectors.why: Conflict raises transport and insurance risk for Ethiopia's best-known export. Its exact route risks are not quantified in our sources.
About 4 million people need urgent aid and access is contested.

sectors.sector: Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb shipping
sectors.why: A fight over Assab would add risk to a route already strained by the Iran war, but no shipping disruption is reported yet.
Two armed states in open confrontation raise demand. We have no sourced figures.
War spending and trade risk usually weigh on an import-dependent economy. This is a general judgement, not sourced to the articles.
EUDR compliance applies to large and medium operators from 30 December 2026, and supply uncertainty from northern Ethiopia adds to costs.

dailyLife.effect: Ethiopian beans could get scarcer or pricier for roasters if exports are disrupted, while EUDR paperwork raises the cost of EU coffee imports from 30 December 2026.
About 4 million people in Tigray need urgent aid. Fighting complicates every convoy and flight.
A second Red Sea flashpoint adds risk to freight costs that have been elevated since the Iran war began on 28 February 2026.
If the war widens, people and arms may move into eastern Sudan, where famine risk is already rising.

scenarios.name: Frozen standoff with insurgency
scenarios.looksLike: Federal forces hold Mekelle and Adigrat, the alliance fights on as an insurgency, Eritrean forces stay near the border and rhetoric stays hot without a formal war.
signposts: No major battle between the two national armies
scenarios.effectOnWorld: A chronic humanitarian crisis, background risk to Red Sea trade and steady pressure on aid budgets.

scenarios.name: Open interstate war
scenarios.looksLike: Direct clashes between the Ethiopian and Eritrean armies, possibly around the border or Assab, with air strikes and mass displacement.
signposts: Strikes on ports or the coast
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Higher shipping and insurance risk at the Red Sea approach, large refugee flows into Sudan and a deeper aid funding gap.

scenarios.name: Mediated de-escalation
scenarios.looksLike: African Union, Gulf or UN mediation produces a pause, talks and possibly restored contact.
signposts: A named envoy and a first meeting
Eritrean forces pull back from Tigray
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Calmer Red Sea risk and better aid access, though underlying disputes remain.

scenarios.name: Alliance collapse and federal consolidation
scenarios.looksLike: The rebel alliance fragments, federal forces take the remaining towns and Eritrea withdraws or is pushed out.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Short-term stabilisation inside Ethiopia but a tense, armed border and unresolved port dispute.

predictions.text: The Ethiopia-Eritrea dispute will not produce a formal peace or restored diplomatic ties (probability about 0.9).
The UN Security Council will hold at least one more meeting or issue a statement on the dispute, but will not adopt sanctions (probability about 0.7).
Ethiopian and Eritrean regular forces will clash in a reported direct engagement beyond the current Tigray front (probability about 0.3).
The Tigray humanitarian caseload will still be at least 4 million in need of urgent aid (probability about 0.7).
A shipping or port disruption in the Assab area will be reported (probability about 0.2).

actions: Map where Ethiopian coffee or other Horn of Africa inputs enter your supply chain, and identify alternates.
Add war-risk and force-majeure language to contracts touching the region.
Prepare EUDR documentation for coffee well before 30 December 2026 so disruption does not compound compliance risk.
Treat this as a tail risk to Red Sea shipping, not a current market driver, until fighting touches ports.
Watch freight and insurance quotes for the Red Sea route for early signals.
Do not assume diplomacy will hold: ties are already cut.
Expect little direct effect on prices unless coffee supply or shipping disruptions grow.
If you want to help, give through established humanitarian agencies working in Tigray and Sudan.
Back quiet mediation by the African Union and regional states before the dispute hardens further.
Press for humanitarian corridors into Tigray.
Plan for refugee flows into eastern Sudan and for the aid funding gap there.

analogues.whatFollowed: Years of 'no war, no peace' after a costly conflict, until the 2018 peace deal.
A devastating conflict that ended with the Pretoria agreement, which left key questions open.
Normalised relations and a Nobel Peace Prize for Abiy in 2019, now unravelled.

evidence.method: Drafted from the event summary, the two listed articles (Al Jazeera, 9 October, and The New Humanitarian, 12 October) and the already-judged connections to other dossiers. Only the headlines and summary were available, so details of the incursions, casualties and diplomatic exchanges are limited. General historical context was used where highly confident. Scenario probabilities, prediction probabilities and sector impacts are estimates and are labelled as such in the text and in the confidence entries.
